kaigo-atomic-nonverbal-dialogue.heading: Adapt listening posture, distance and touch to the person
paragraphs: Expressions and movements provide important information for understanding someone. However, the same gesture can have several meanings. Do not establish feelings from expression alone; check alongside the person’s words and the situation.

Facing the person and matching eye level rather than looking down can reduce a sense of pressure. Check how much eye contact feels comfortable. Do not conclude that avoiding eye contact means they are not listening or require continuous eye contact to demonstrate understanding.

A slow, calm voice and pauses for replies help the person receive information and respond. A worker’s nods and brief acknowledgments show listening. However, one nod from the person does not establish understanding and consent to specific assistance. Check necessary details separately.

Crossed arms or legs and leaning away can sometimes make someone seem difficult to approach. Meanings vary with culture, individuals and physical conditions. Rather than judging personality from one posture, face the person, adopt a comfortable position and check their response.

Some people find close distance or holding hands reassuring; others find it unpleasant. Cultural knowledge does not replace asking this person’s wishes. Responses to touch also vary with timing, force and frequency. Explain the purpose and check an acceptable approach; stop that contact if it is declined.

Learning case: the person steps away when a worker approaches. Rather than approaching again because ‘everyone here is friendly,’ keep a comfortable distance and ask where they would prefer you to speak. Explain and confirm the purpose and method even when touch is needed for assistance.
This unit teaches meanings and reasons for checking. Actual support follows condition, wishes, the individual plan and facility guidance. Do not independently begin a method that is unclear.

kaigo-atomic-shared-care-records.heading: Pass condition, assistance and responses to the next worker
paragraphs: Sharing information with healthcare and other professionals as well as care workers supports the person’s life as a team. Records do more than fill forms: they improve support quality and enable necessary checks and assistance to continue when responsibility changes.

Plans describe future support, case records preserve its course, and handovers convey necessary information to the next worker. Consultation also occurs in meetings or direct conversation, but speaking alone does not create every required record. Keep planned and implemented support distinct.

Record on the same day as promptly as possible, following facility procedures, so the event’s timing is clear. Do not confuse event and writing times if they differ. Record condition, assistance actually provided and subsequent response separately.

Distinguish sources for the person’s words ‘it hurts,’ observed skin changes and measured values. When relaying a healthcare professional’s assessment, identify whose judgment it is rather than implying diagnosis from a worker’s observation alone. Do not invent unconfirmed values or responses to make a record look complete.

Recipients also note key points, repeat what was heard and ask about uncertainties. Sharing what is handed over and who checks next helps identify omissions and misunderstandings. Handle information with appropriate recipients in appropriate places; do not spread private matters to uninvolved people.

Learning case: a handover saying only ‘everything is fine’ does not tell the recipient what was done or which response was checked. Supply actual times, condition, assistance, responses and unconfirmed matters specifically, and confirm next checks and responsibilities.
This unit teaches meanings and reasons for checking. Actual support follows condition, wishes, the individual plan and facility guidance. Do not independently begin a method that is unclear.

kaigo-atomic-movement-body-labels.heading: Describe body locations and sides specifically
paragraphs: Muscles, bones and joints contribute to body movement. To describe locations, distinguish the head, neck, chest, abdomen, back, lower back and buttocks. Rather than summarizing everything as bodily distress, checking where the person points helps reporting.

In the upper limbs, distinguish shoulder, arm, elbow, wrist, palm and back of the hand. Use left and right from the person’s body, not reversed from the facing worker’s viewpoint. Also check the indicated location on the back of the hand, opposite the palm, with the person before reporting.

In the lower limbs, distinguish leg, knee, ankle, heel and sole. The sole means the foot’s underside, not just the heel. Separate the person’s indicated location, onset and sensations from what the worker actually observes.

Knowing a body-area name differs from knowing a diagnosis or suitable transfer method. Check pain, movement range, independent abilities and the plan, and communicate to necessary recipients. Do not independently pull limbs to investigate a disease while trying to identify a location.

Learning case: saying ‘my hand hurts,’ the person points to the back of their right hand. Ask whether that is the correct location, and record it, the time and their words. Observe visible changes separately; do not add a guessed pain cause.
This unit teaches meanings and reasons for checking. Actual support follows condition, wishes, the individual plan and facility guidance. Do not independently begin a method that is unclear.

kaigo-atomic-visual-guided-walking.heading: Share pace and route changes in advance
paragraphs: When guiding someone with limited sight, first speak and introduce yourself, then ask whether help is wanted and how they want to be guided. Match their pace rather than pulling at a speed convenient for staff. Check equipment, abilities and route before moving.

Describe corners, steps and floor changes before reaching them. Agree on references such as directions from the person’s viewpoint and communicate specifically so they can anticipate and adjust movements. An explanation only after turning arrives too late to help preparation.

The textbook’s guiding posture illustrates checking wishes and sharing support. Do not assume everyone wants identical contact. Adapt to wishes, facility-trained methods and responses during movement. Do not suddenly grab an arm or pull without checking wishes.

Learning case: a worker first pulls the person around a corner and explains afterward. Next time, communicate direction and changes before the corner, check pace and guiding method, and then proceed. If route or assistance conditions are unsuitable, stop and check another method or necessary help.
This unit teaches meanings and reasons for checking. Actual support follows condition, wishes, the individual plan and facility guidance. Do not independently begin a method that is unclear.

kaigo-language-session-1-notes.heading: Read suggestions, responsibilities and sequences
paragraphs: In learning dialogue209, the window seat is the worker’s suggestion; the person prefers a seat near the entrance. They still intend to attend the afternoon gathering and not go into the garden. Do not retain the suggested window seat as their final choice or report that the whole activity is canceled.

‘I wrote it’ identifies the speaker as the writer. ‘I had a senior colleague check it’ includes a separate person’s action: the senior colleague checked it. Distinguish who entered the checklist number, who checked results and who will sign. Completed entry and checking do not necessarily mean signing is complete.

The reservation-change dialogue hinges on ‘ask reception first’ and ‘tell you after I know a change is possible.’ Wishing to go earlier, confirming a change is possible and actually departing are separate states. Telling a colleague the plan also does not mean changing or departing is complete.

‘First, next, afterward’ describe the order of the current task. In dialogue212, check the date, show the person responsible, then display the notice. If the initial repeat-back is wrong, read through the correction. Do not transfer this notice-posting order to another assistance procedure such as a transfer.

When relaying a negative expression such as ‘not bad,’ preserve the degree the person stated. Do not strengthen it to ‘very good’ or extend it to absence of every problem. Ask if concerns or their degree need checking. ‘Not very’ or ‘not often’ means a degree or frequency is not high. For example, do not change ‘doesn’t talk much’ into ‘never talks.’

kaigo-reading-new-209.heading: Learning dialogue: distinguish seat preferences from participation
paragraphs:
Resident: I will attend the afternoon gathering, but I won’t go into the garden.
Worker: Shall I arrange a seat by the window?
Resident: It is bright there, so I would prefer a seat near the entrance.
Worker: Near the entrance. I will check the venue now.
Resident: Thank you. I haven’t canceled my participation.
Worker: Yes, only your seat preference has changed.

Reading check: participation in the afternoon gathering is not canceled. The person will not go into the garden and prefers the entrance rather than the worker’s suggested window seat. The worker will check the venue next, so the seat cannot be read as already arranged.

kaigo-reading-new-210.heading: Learning dialogue: distinguish entry, checking and signing roles
paragraphs:
Worker A: Is the wheelchair checklist complete?
Worker B: I wrote the number. I had a senior colleague check the results.
Worker A: So everything is finished?
Worker B: No, it has not been signed yet.
Worker A: Who will sign?
Worker B: I will ask the senior colleague who checked it.

Reading check: Worker B wrote the number; the senior colleague checked the results. Signing remains undone, and B plans to ask the colleague who checked. Separate actions and roles: having someone check does not mean checking it yourself or completing a signature. This learning dialogue about a checklist does not instruct actual wheelchair inspection.

kaigo-reading-new-211.heading: Learning dialogue: do not finalize a change before checking possibility
paragraphs:
Resident: I would like to go to the library earlier.
Worker: First I will ask reception whether the reservation can be changed.
Resident: Are we leaving right now?
Worker: No. I will let you know after I find out a change is possible.
Resident: I understand. I will wait for your reply.
Worker: I will also tell another worker about the plan.

Reading check: the worker first plans to ask reception whether the reservation can change, then inform the person once a change is known to be possible. The person waits for a reply. There is no evidence of completed time changes or departure; saying a colleague will be told the plan also does not make it completed.

kaigo-reading-new-212.heading: Learning dialogue: read the corrected task sequence
paragraphs:
Worker A: Please prepare the notice. First check the date, then show it to the person responsible. We will display it afterward.
Worker B: So we show them after displaying it?
Worker A: Those two are the other way round.
Worker B: Date check, responsible person’s check, then display?
Worker A: Yes. Please follow that order for this notice.
Worker B: I will display it last.

Reading check: this notice requires checking the date, showing the person responsible, then displaying it. Worker B initially reversed showing and displaying but finally corrected display to last. This order applies only to the notice request, not other tasks or care movements.

kaigo-language-session-1-terms.heading: Vocabulary for dialogue roles and plans
paragraphs: 希望（きぼう） — Wishes: what the person would like to do or have happen.
提案（ていあん） — Suggestion: putting forward an idea for the other person to consider. Distinguish it from their chosen outcome.
確認（かくにん） — Checking: asking or investigating uncertainty to establish reliable information.
参加（さんか） — Participation: joining a gathering or similar activity. Check this separately from seating or location preferences.
点検表（てんけんひょう） — Checklist: a table recording equipment checks or their results. Its existence alone does not establish completed inspection.
署名（しょめい） — Signature: writing one’s name. This differs from entering a number or checking results.
予約（よやく） — Reservation: applying in advance to use something. Check separately whether a change is possible and whether it is complete.
受付（うけつけ） — Reception: the desk or person handling applications and inquiries. In the dialogue, it is where the worker asks whether a change is possible.
掲示（けいじ） — Displaying a notice where people can see it. In this dialogue, it is planned after checks are complete.
順序（じゅんじょ） — Sequence: which action comes before or after another. Include corrected parts when checking.

kaigo-language-session-2-notes.heading: Read request scope, meal amounts and display conditions
paragraphs: Check the meaning of 下げる from its object and context. 食器を下げる means clearing used dishes; ズボンを下げる means lowering trousers. 冷ます means cooling something; 温める means warming it. Reading a word does not establish a suitable temperature or cooking method for the person.

嚥下 means swallowing; 誤嚥 means food, liquids or other material entering the airway below the vocal cords. General swallowing difficulty and aspiration are not identical. むせる and 咳込む describe reactions or the person’s own words, but these terms alone do not diagnose causes or aspiration or authorize independently changing thickening.

献立 is the combination of dishes; 献立表 is the menu showing them. Record intake of staple food, side dishes and soup separately. ‘All the staple food, half the side dishes’ does not mean unconfirmed soup was all consumed too. 焼き魚 is grilled fish, あげもの is deep-fried food, and いためもの is stir-fried food. Names alone do not establish prescribed amounts.

Practice explaining: distinguish とろみ from とろみ粉. The former is a liquid’s thickness; the latter is material used to adjust it. Next, write one sentence recording soup intake as unknown. Example: ‘All the staple food and half the side dishes were consumed. Soup intake remains unconfirmed; the record will be corrected after checking.’

kaigo-reading-new-215.heading: Learning dialogue: distinguish independent actions from requested reading
paragraphs:
Resident: I would like to open the snack bag myself.
Worker: I will put it here, then.
Resident: The name label is too small to read. Please just read that part.
Worker: I will read the label and hand you the bag unopened.
Resident: Yes. I want to know what the snack is before eating.
Worker: Understood.

Reading check: the person wants to open the bag themselves. The only help requested is reading the small name label. The worker plans to hand it over unopened. Difficulty seeing text does not establish inability to eat, chew or swallow.

kaigo-reading-new-216.heading: Learning dialogue: separate staple food, side-dish and soup amounts
paragraphs:
Worker A: I am checking the lunch record. Were both the staple food and side dishes half eaten?
Worker B: All the staple food and half the side dishes were eaten.
Worker A: What about the soup?
Worker B: I haven’t checked yet.
Worker A: Then please don’t write that everything was eaten.
Worker B: I will correct the record after checking soup intake.

Reading check: all staple food and half the side dishes are confirmed, but soup intake remains unchecked. Worker B plans to correct the record after checking soup. Neither consumption of every dish nor completed correction is stated.

kaigo-reading-new-217.heading: Learning dialogue: preserve weekday conditions and undecided choices
paragraphs:
Resident: Can I choose snack time next week too?
Worker: You can choose the time only on Wednesdays.
Resident: Can I also choose my dining-room seat only on that day?
Worker: We ask your seat preference every day.
Resident: Then I will have Wednesday’s snack at three. I want to choose the seat on the day.
Worker: Three for the time, and the seat is still undecided.

Reading check: at this fictional facility, snack time can be chosen only on Wednesdays, while seat preferences are asked daily. The person chose three o’clock for Wednesday’s snack. The seat remains undecided because they want to choose on the day. Do not merge the weekday condition with the daily preference check.

kaigo-reading-new-218.heading: Learning dialogue: check both paper and large print
paragraphs:
Resident: I would like to see the menu. Is there a paper version printed in large letters?
Worker: We can enlarge the text on a tablet.
Resident: I would prefer paper, not a screen.
Worker: A small-print paper menu would be hard to read.
Resident: Yes. I need both conditions.
Worker: I will check whether a large-print version is available.

Reading check: the person needs a paper menu with large print. Enlarged text on a screen does not meet the paper requirement; small print on paper does not meet readability needs. The worker will check availability of a suitable printout; it has not already been secured and handed over.

kaigo-language-session-2-terms.heading: Vocabulary to consult when needed
paragraphs: 温める（あたためる） — To warm something by raising its temperature.
エプロン（えぷろん） — Apron: worn to protect clothing or similar surfaces from soiling.
嚥下（えんげ） — Swallowing: moving material from the mouth through the throat toward the esophagus.
きざむ（きざむ） — To chop food or other material finely.
誤嚥（ごえん） — Aspiration: food, drink or saliva entering the airway below the vocal folds.
こぼす（こぼす） — To spill food or liquid outside a container.
下げる（さげる） — In “clear the dishes,” this means removing used tableware.
冷ます（さます） — To cool something hot.
食品（しょくひん） — Food products used for eating or drinking.
食欲（しょくよく） — Appetite: the desire to eat.
水分補給（すいぶんほきゅう） — Replacing the fluids the body needs. Follow the person’s plan for how and how much to drink.
咳込む（せきこむ） — To cough repeatedly.
とろみ（とろみ） — Thickness or viscosity of a liquid. The term is not permission for a care worker to change it freely.
粉（こな） — Powder: fine particles. As a standalone word it is generally read kona. In the course expression とろみ（粉）, the reading ko is supplied for 粉, referring to powder used to adjust thickness.
つける（つける） — In “add thickness,” this means making a liquid more viscous.
飲み込む（のみこむ） — To swallow: moving material from the mouth through the throat into the esophagus.
一口大（ひとくちだい） — Bite-sized: small enough to fit in the mouth in one bite. It does not define the same suitable amount for everyone.
むせる（むせる） — A coughing response during eating or similar situations. This alone does not establish whether aspiration occurred.
量（りょう） — Amount: how much there is. Specify whether it is eaten or left over.
リーダー（りーだー） — Team leader: the person coordinating the team’s work.
記録（きろく） — Recording observations, statements and completed actions separately.
あげもの（あげもの） — Deep-fried dishes.
いためもの（いためもの） — Stir-fried dishes: ingredients heated while moved in a small amount of oil.
おやつ（おやつ） — A snack between main meals, or snack time.
粥（かゆ） — Rice porridge or a similar grain cooked in plenty of water. Its name alone does not establish suitability for swallowing.
お粥（おかゆ） — Polite form of 粥, meaning rice porridge.
カレーライス（かれーらいす） — Curry rice: rice served with curry beside or over it.
献立（こんだて） — Menu: the combination of dishes provided for a meal.
献立表（こんだてひょう） — A chart listing dishes for each meal.
主食（しゅしょく） — Staple food: a grain-based main component such as rice or bread.
汁物（しるもの） — Soup or another dish containing broth, such as miso soup.
ゼリー（ぜりー） — Gel dessert: a food made by setting a liquid. The name alone does not establish swallowing suitability.
たまご焼き（たまごやき） — A dish made by beating and cooking eggs.
漬物（つけもの） — Pickles: vegetables or other ingredients preserved in salt or seasoned liquid.
天ぷら（てんぷら） — Tempura: ingredients coated in batter and deep-fried.
豆腐（とうふ） — Tofu: a soybean food made by setting soy milk.
丼（どんぶり） — A large, deep bowl, or a dish of rice topped with ingredients in such a bowl. Use context to distinguish the meanings.
煮付け（につけ） — Simmering ingredients in seasoned liquid to absorb flavor, or a dish prepared this way.
煮物（にもの） — A dish simmered with liquid and seasonings.
ハンバーグ（はんばーぐ） — Hamburger steak: ground meat and other ingredients shaped and cooked.
副食（ふくしょく） — Side dishes eaten with the staple.
プリン（ぷりん） — A set dessert such as custard made with eggs and milk. Check ingredients for each product.
麦茶（むぎちゃ） — Barley tea: a drink made from barley.
メニュー（めにゅー） — A list of dishes offered; may refer to the meal plan.
焼き魚（やきざかな） — Grilled fish.
ヨーグルト（よーぐると） — Yogurt: a food made by fermenting milk or similar ingredients.

kaigo-language-session-3-notes.heading: Separate elimination vocabulary, consent and information scope
paragraphs: 尿 and 尿意 distinguish urine from the urge to urinate; 便 and 便意 distinguish stool from the urge to defecate. 尿器 is a urinal, 便座 the toilet seat, and ポータブルトイレ a movable commode. Knowing names alone does not determine suitable methods or positioning.

ズボンを上げる・下げる means moving trousers up or down. Without an object, clarify rather than confusing it with contexts such as clearing dishes. 羞恥心 means embarrassment. Do not assume everyone feels identically in the same situation; adapt conversation location and exposure scope to the person.

看護師 is read かんごし, nurse; 職員 is read しょくいん, staff member. Not every facility worker is a nurse: check the responsible role when contacting someone. Recognize 浣腸 as the word for an enema, but learning the term provides neither training nor authority to perform one.

Practice explaining: are ‘the person reported an urge to urinate’ and ‘urination was confirmed’ the same? The former is a reported sensation; the latter confirms that urine actually passed. Do not infer one from the other. Record separately what was heard and what was confirmed.

kaigo-reading-new-220.heading: Learning dialogue: distinguish an unsuitable location from declining discussion
paragraphs:
Resident: I want to discuss toileting, but not here.
Worker: There are people around. May I listen somewhere else?
Resident: Yes. I haven’t told my family yet.
Worker: After listening, I will explain any necessary information sharing.
Resident: Please don’t tell everyone first.
Worker: Understood. First I will check the location.

Reading check: the person has not declined the discussion itself; they do not want to speak in the current public setting. Family has not yet been told. The worker will check a location first, listen, then explain necessary sharing. Do not infer that anyone has already been told or that unconditional secrecy in every circumstance was promised.

kaigo-reading-new-221.heading: Learning dialogue: check current explanation scope against the final request
paragraphs:
Resident: Please explain the call button tomorrow.
Worker: Understood. You want to rest now.
Resident: But I would like to know now just who is notified when I press it.
Worker: May I briefly explain only that point?
Resident: Yes. Please leave the other explanations until tomorrow.
Worker: Just the notification recipient for now.

Reading check: the initial wish was to postpone the button explanation until tomorrow. The person then asked to learn only the notification recipient now. Permission for the current explanation covers that brief point only; other explanations remain for tomorrow. Preserve the finally confirmed scope, not just an intermediate statement.

kaigo-reading-new-222.heading: Learning dialogue: distinguish writing difficulty from conveying information
paragraphs:
Resident: I would like to write the time in my toileting record.
Worker: Could you write it here?
Resident: I cannot write with a pen, but I remember the time.
Worker: Could you tell me aloud? I will write it and read it back.
Resident: Please do it that way.
Worker: I will ask you the time now.

Reading check: the person cannot write with a pen but remembers the time and wants to participate in the record. They agreed to tell the worker aloud, have it written, and check it through read-back. The time has yet to be asked, so record-content confirmation is not complete. Do not assume why they cannot write or that memory is impaired.

kaigo-reading-new-223.heading: Learning dialogue: distinguish the two buttons on this device
paragraphs:
Worker A: This manual describes a confirm button and a call button.
Worker B: Does pressing confirm bring a worker?
Worker A: No. Confirm only closes the display. Call notifies staff.
Worker B: That describes this device?
Worker A: Yes. Check each other device’s own manual.
Worker B: We won’t assume functions from names alone.

Reading check: on this learning-example device, confirm closes the display and call notifies staff. Notification is not evidence that a worker has already arrived. Check other devices’ own manuals; the same button name does not guarantee the same function.

kaigo-language-session-3-terms.heading: Vocabulary to consult when needed
paragraphs: 上げる（あげる） — Raise: here, returning lowered clothing upward, as in pulling up pants.
足元（あしもと） — Feet and the area around them: check that clothing or equipment is not obstructing movement around the feet.
陰部（いんぶ） — Genital area: the external genitals and surrounding area. Respect privacy, check the necessary extent of care and minimize exposure.
おむつ（おむつ） — Diaper: an item worn to collect urine or stool. Its use does not establish the person’s overall abilities.
浣腸（かんちょう） — Enema: a procedure introducing liquid or another substance through the anus to encourage a bowel movement. Learning this word does not authorize you to perform it yourself.
着替える（きがえる） — Change clothes: take off the clothing being worn and put on other clothing.
下げる（さげる） — Lower: here, moving clothing downward, as in lowering pants.
失禁（しっきん） — Incontinence: urine or stool escaping involuntarily. It is not a reason to blame the person.
羞恥心（しゅうちしん） — Embarrassment: feeling embarrassed about being seen or having something known. Ask the person how they feel.
使い捨て手袋（つかいすててぶくろ） — Disposable gloves: gloves intended for one use. Remove them appropriately after dirty tasks and perform hand hygiene.
尿（にょう） — Urine: liquid produced by the kidneys that passes through the ureters, bladder and urethra to leave the body.
尿器（にょうき） — Urinal: a device for collecting urine. Knowing about a device is different from being able to select and use it appropriately.
尿意（にょうい） — Urge to urinate: the feeling of wanting to pass urine.
排泄（はいせつ） — Excretion: removing substances the body no longer needs. It includes urine and stool and also relates to processes such as sweating.
便（べん） — Stool: material that passes through the large intestine and other parts after digestion and absorption and leaves through the anus.
便意（べんい） — Urge to have a bowel movement: the feeling of wanting to pass stool.
便座（べんざ） — Toilet seat: the sitting surface that supports the body when using a toilet.
ポータブルトイレ（ポータブルトイレ） — Portable toilet: a movable toilet used in places such as a person’s room. Use it in a way appropriate to their condition and plan.
看護師（かんごし） — Nurse: a professional providing nursing care and assisting medical treatment. Report confirmed facts and consult them about changes in condition.
職員（しょくいん） — Staff member: a person working in the facility or organization. Distinguish people’s responsibilities when contacting them.
パジャマ（ぱじゃま） — Pajamas: clothing worn for sleep and similar occasions.
呼び出しボタン（よびだしボタン） — Call button: a button signaling that a staff member is needed. Check that it works, is within reach and the person understands and can use it.

141.title: Respect listening posture and personal boundaries
objectives: Do not assign one fixed meaning to expressions, gaze or posture.
Ask about distance and touch preferences, and check understanding and consent separately.
141.context: Consider someone stepping away when a worker approaches. Practice checking their current preferred distance and manner of conversation rather than relying on cultural generalities.
141.artCaption: Check wishes through words, expressions and pointing together. One gesture alone does not establish understanding or consent.

142.title: Leave records that let the next worker continue support
objectives: Record condition, actual assistance and personal responses separately.
Identify sources and unconfirmed matters, and check the recipient’s understanding and role.
142.context: Consider how “everything is fine” alone fails to convey assistance and checked responses. Confirm necessary facts rather than adding unknown values or assessments.
142.artCaption: Hand over in a quiet place; the recipient also checks through notes and questions. Distinguish speaking from sharing understanding.

143.title: Describe body areas from the person’s viewpoint
objectives: Distinguish trunk, upper-limb and lower-limb areas and sides.
Confirm the indicated location and complaint and report separately from guessed causes.
143.context: Consider checking and reporting “my hand hurts” when the person points to the back of their right hand. Knowing location does not establish diagnosis or a transfer method.
143.artCaption: Check the indicated body area and specifically ask about sides, time and sensations. Do not apply the pictured location to every case.

144.title: Respect pace and advance notice when guiding someone with limited sight
objectives: Check preferred guiding methods and route conditions before moving.
Describe corners and steps specifically before reaching them and adapt to responses.
144.context: Review pulling a hand around a corner without warning and explaining afterward. This learns prerequisites for safe movement and checks wishes; it does not instruct trying unfamiliar guiding.
144.artCaption: Introduce yourself and speak first, then check the desired guiding method. Share pace and route changes.

145.title: Read wishes, responsibilities and order in conversations
objectives: Separate suggestions from personal choices and responsible people from completed tasks.
Distinguish plans conditional on checks from completed facts.
145.context: Read four learning dialogues about seats, checklist signatures, reservation changes and notice order. Do not infer unstated completed movement or secured seats.
145.artCaption: Listen to wishes and check abilities, environment and plans together. Consultation is not a record of completed movement.

146.title: Read meal information and personal requests accurately
objectives: Separate assistance scope, known intake and unconfirmed amounts.
Preserve weekday and display-method conditions and undecided details.
146.context: The learning dialogues cover who opens a bag, meal amounts, weekday choices and menu format. Do not use vocabulary to diagnose or independently choose food textures.
146.artCaption: Record information for each dish separately from amounts actually confirmed. A container’s presence alone establishes neither intake nor completed serving.

147.title: Distinguish toileting discussions, consent and device functions
objectives: Check discussion locations and the scope of explanation permitted now.
Distinguish writing difficulty from memory and button names from actual functions.
147.context: Read learning dialogues about discussion location, explanation scope, checking written assistance and fictional button functions. Do not infer another device’s functions or the person’s abilities.
147.artCaption: Consider location and nearby people when discussing toileting. Wanting a discussion does not necessarily mean wanting it here and now.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-nonverbal-dialo.prompt: The person steps back when a worker approaches. A colleague says, ‘Everyone in this region prefers close distances.’ What is appropriate?
options: Keep a comfortable distance and ask where the person would prefer you to speak.
Approach to the same distance again to convey friendliness.
Decide never to speak to them again because they stepped back.
Explain the regional tendency and have them become accustomed to close distances.
rationales: This checks the person’s current response and wishes rather than relying on cultural generalities.
This repeats the approach without checking the response of stepping away.
A distance preference does not establish rejection of conversation itself.
Cultural tendencies do not justify making someone accept an approach.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-shared-care-rec.prompt: A handover says only ‘everything is fine,’ leaving assistance and responses unclear. What review is needed?
options: Fill unconfirmed measurements with standard values to reassure the next worker.
Replace ‘fine’ with ‘no abnormalities’ instead of supplying details.
Omit required records and recipient checks because the handover was spoken.
Check and add actual times, condition, assistance, responses and unconfirmed matters, and agree on next checks with the recipient.
rationales: Do not invent unmeasured values to make a record complete.
Changing expressions still does not convey what assistance or checks occurred.
Speaking differs from completing necessary records and sharing understanding.
This specifies actual information and includes checks supporting continued care.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-movement-body-l.prompt: The handover says ‘arm pain,’ but the person points to the back of their right hand. What should be checked?
options: Record the facing worker’s right as the person’s right.
Confirm the back of the person’s right hand, and report the time, words and observations separately from assumptions.
Diagnose the cause from the indicated location and hand over a disease name.
Omit the indicated location because ‘arm’ includes the hand.
rationales: Avoid confusing left and right when facing someone; check from the person’s side.
This checks personal left/right and the specific location while separating sources.
Location alone does not diagnose the cause of pain.
A broad area label loses the specific location the person indicated.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-visual-guided-w.prompt: A worker pulls someone with limited sight around a corner and explains the corner afterward. What needs changing?
options: Check the desired guiding method and pace, and explain direction and other details before turning.
A detailed explanation afterward removes the need for advance warning.
Knowing the route removes the need to ask wishes.
Omit corners and steps and always maintain the same speed.
rationales: This combines advance notice, wishes and pace, checking before movement.
An explanation after movement does not replace advance information needed to prepare for change.
Route knowledge differs from checking a personally suitable guiding method.
Check pace too, adapting to route changes and personal responses.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-209.prompt: Which matches the person’s wishes and the worker’s next action?
options: The person wants a window seat, which is already arranged.
Not going into the garden means not attending the afternoon gathering.
The person will attend the afternoon gathering and prefers a seat near the entrance. The worker will check the venue.
Any seat is acceptable, so the worker will guide them without checking.
rationales: The window seat was a suggestion, not the final preference. Its availability is unconfirmed too.
This confuses not going into the garden with canceling attendance.
This separates attendance, seating preference and a check not yet carried out.
The person prefers the entrance, and the worker says they will check.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-209.reading:
Resident: I will attend the afternoon gathering, but I won’t go into the garden.
Worker: Shall I arrange a seat by the window?
Resident: It is bright there, so I would prefer a seat near the entrance.
Worker: Near the entrance. I will check the venue now.
Resident: Thank you. I haven’t canceled my participation.
Worker: Yes, only your seat preference has changed.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-210.prompt: Which statement about entering, checking and signing the checklist matches the dialogue?
options: Worker B entered the number and checked the results; the senior colleague has already signed.
Worker B entered the number and the senior colleague checked results. Asking the colleague to sign is still to come.
The senior colleague entered the number; Worker B checked results and signed.
The senior colleague’s check removes any need to ask for a signature.
rationales: This changes who checked and turns the unfinished signature into completion.
This accurately preserves roles and unfinished parts of the three actions.
The writer and checker are reversed, and a completed signature is not stated.
Completed checking and a plan to request a signature can both be true.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-210.reading:
Worker A: Is the wheelchair checklist complete?
Worker B: I wrote the number. I had a senior colleague check the results.
Worker A: So everything is finished?
Worker B: No, it has not been signed yet.
Worker A: Who will sign?
Worker B: I will ask the senior colleague who checked it.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-211.prompt: Which matches the current stage of the reservation change?
options: Reception has confirmed, and the person has departed at the changed time.
The wish alone finalized the change without asking reception.
Saying a colleague will be told the plan means the person has already received the result.
The worker will ask reception whether a change is possible and inform the person afterward. The person will wait for a reply.
rationales: This turns checking and departure into completed facts not in the dialogue.
A wish alone does not establish possibility; reception will be asked.
Sharing a plan with a colleague and notifying the person of results are separate actions.
Checking possibility and notifying the person are still pending, distinct from a completed change.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-211.reading:
Resident: I would like to go to the library earlier.
Worker: First I will ask reception whether the reservation can be changed.
Resident: Are we leaving right now?
Worker: No. I will let you know after I find out a change is possible.
Resident: I understand. I will wait for your reply.
Worker: I will also tell another worker about the plan.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-212.prompt: What notice-preparation order was finally confirmed?
options: Check the date, display it, then show the person responsible.
Show the person responsible, display it, then check the date.
Check the date, show the person responsible, then display it.
Display it, then check the date and responsible person later.
rationales: This is the mistaken intermediate order, corrected at the end.
This moves the initial date check to the end.
This reflects the final correction: showing the person responsible comes before display.
Display is last, not before checks.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-212.reading:
Worker A: Please prepare the notice. First check the date, then show it to the person responsible. We will display it afterward.
Worker B: So we show them after displaying it?
Worker A: Those two are the other way round.
Worker B: Date check, responsible person’s check, then display?
Worker A: Yes. Please follow that order for this notice.
Worker B: I will display it last.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-215.prompt: What assistance did the person ask the worker for?
options: Read the small name label while the person opens the bag themselves.
Open the bag and remove the contents before reading the name.
Take over all eating actions because text is hard to see.
Have the person both read the name and open the bag alone.
rationales: This preserves both reading assistance and the wish to open the bag independently.
The person wants to open the bag and did not request opening help.
Difficulty seeing text does not establish eating ability or necessary assistance.
Opening is the person’s action, but reading the name was requested from staff.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-215.reading:
Resident: I would like to open the snack bag myself.
Worker: I will put it here, then.
Resident: The name label is too small to read. Please just read that part.
Worker: I will read the label and hand you the bag unopened.
Resident: Yes. I want to know what the snack is before eating.
Worker: Understood.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-216.prompt: Which correctly describes intake and the record?
options: All staple food, side dishes and soup were confirmed eaten.
Half the staple food, all side dishes and no soup were consumed.
Soup intake is unknown, but the record correction is already complete.
All staple food and half the side dishes were consumed; soup is unconfirmed. The record will be corrected after checking.
rationales: Side dishes were half consumed, and soup intake remains unchecked.
Staple and side-dish amounts are reversed, and no soup intake is not established.
Worker B plans correction after checking soup and does not say it is complete.
This separates each dish’s amount and the pending record correction.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-216.reading:
Worker A: I am checking the lunch record. Were both the staple food and side dishes half eaten?
Worker B: All the staple food and half the side dishes were eaten.
Worker A: What about the soup?
Worker B: I haven’t checked yet.
Worker A: Then please don’t write that everything was eaten.
Worker B: I will correct the record after checking soup intake.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-217.prompt: Which matches the preference checks at this learning-example facility?
options: Snack time is set to three every day, and seats are asked about only on Wednesday.
Wednesday’s snack is set for three, while the seat will be chosen on the day. Seat preferences are asked daily.
Wednesday’s snack and seat are both already decided.
Choosing a seat on Wednesday means snack time cannot be chosen.
rationales: This changes both the day for time choice and the frequency of seat checks.
This distinguishes the weekday-limited time choice from daily seat-preference checks.
Time is chosen, but the seat remains undecided until the day.
Wednesday’s snack time can be chosen, and the preference of three has been stated.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-217.reading:
Resident: Can I choose snack time next week too?
Worker: You can choose the time only on Wednesdays.
Resident: Can I also choose my dining-room seat only on that day?
Worker: We ask your seat preference every day.
Resident: Then I will have Wednesday’s snack at three. I want to choose the seat on the day.
Worker: Three for the time, and the seat is still undecided.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-218.prompt: Which menu meets the person’s conditions?
options: A large-print paper menu. The worker will check whether it can be provided.
A menu with large text on a screen rather than paper.
A paper menu with small print.
Any format, treated as already handed over.
rationales: This meets both paper and large-print conditions and preserves the pending check.
Large text meets one condition but not the paper preference.
Paper alone does not meet the request for large print.
There are two conditions, and availability has yet to be checked.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-218.reading:
Resident: I would like to see the menu. Is there a paper version printed in large letters?
Worker: We can enlarge the text on a tablet.
Resident: I would prefer paper, not a screen.
Worker: A small-print paper menu would be hard to read.
Resident: Yes. I need both conditions.
Worker: I will check whether a large-print version is available.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-220.prompt: Which matches the person’s wishes and the worker’s plans for the toileting discussion?
options: The person declined discussion itself, so no location check is needed.
Family has already been told by the person, so the worker will not listen.
Do not discuss it in the current location; check another place first. Explain necessary sharing after listening.
Promise never to share with anyone under any circumstances in exchange for moving.
rationales: The person declined speaking where others are present, not the discussion itself.
The person says family has not yet been told; the worker plans to listen.
This respects location preferences and preserves the pending discussion and sharing explanation.
The dialogue plans an explanation of necessary sharing, not unconditional secrecy.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-220.reading:
Resident: I want to discuss toileting, but not here.
Worker: There are people around. May I listen somewhere else?
Resident: Yes. I haven’t told my family yet.
Worker: After listening, I will explain any necessary information sharing.
Resident: Please don’t tell everyone first.
Worker: Understood. First I will check the location.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-221.prompt: What scope of explanation was finally agreed for now?
options: Explain nothing now, including the recipient, because tomorrow was mentioned first.
Briefly explain only who is notified when pressed; leave the rest until tomorrow.
Explain every other function now because the person wants the recipient explained.
Leave the recipient until tomorrow and explain other uses now.
rationales: This retains only the first wish and drops the later request to know the recipient now.
This reflects the added wish and limits the current explanation to the recipient.
This expands consent to one explanation into consent for all functions.
This reverses what is wanted now and what is postponed.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-221.reading:
Resident: Please explain the call button tomorrow.
Worker: Understood. You want to rest now.
Resident: But I would like to know now just who is notified when I press it.
Worker: May I briefly explain only that point?
Resident: Yes. Please leave the other explanations until tomorrow.
Worker: Just the notification recipient for now.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-222.prompt: Which method and current stage of participation in the record were agreed?
options: Assume memory loss from inability to write and have the worker guess the time.
Have the worker write without reading back and treat it as already confirmed.
The person declined the record, so there is no need to ask the time aloud.
The person will state the time aloud; the worker will write and read it back. Asking the time is still to come.
rationales: Do not infer memory problems from inability to write; ask the time the person remembers.
This omits agreed read-back and changes planned action to completion.
The person wants to participate and agreed to speak the information.
This uses remembered information and accurately preserves the plan to confirm it after writing.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-222.reading:
Resident: I would like to write the time in my toileting record.
Worker: Could you write it here?
Resident: I cannot write with a pen, but I remember the time.
Worker: Could you tell me aloud? I will write it and read it back.
Resident: Please do it that way.
Worker: I will ask you the time now.

weekly-kaigo-reading-new-223.prompt: Which statement about this device’s buttons is correct?
options: Both confirm and call verify that a worker has arrived.
Confirm notifies staff, while call closes the display.
Confirm closes the display and call notifies staff. Notification alone does not establish arrival.
The same button name always means the same function on other devices.
rationales: Neither closing the display nor sending notification was described as checking arrival.
This reverses the two stated functions.
This preserves the functions and distinguishes notification from actual arrival.
This learning-example device’s explanation cannot be generalized to another device.
weekly-kaigo-reading-new-223.reading:
Worker A: This manual describes a confirm button and a call button.
Worker B: Does pressing confirm bring a worker?
Worker A: No. Confirm only closes the display. Call notifies staff.
Worker B: That describes this device?
Worker A: Yes. Check each other device’s own manual.
Worker B: We won’t assume functions from names alone.
